title: Subhash Ghai Just Watched Salman Khan's Maatrubhumi. He Called It a Must-Watch. The Film's Journey to Get Here Is the Real Story.
excerpt: The war drama formerly known as Battle of Galwan was 40% reshot after the Defence Ministry intervened. Subhash Ghai's rough-cut endorsement may be the signal Salman's camp needed.
body:
Subhash Ghai, the man who directed *Taal*, *Pardes*, and *Ram Lakhan*, does not hand out praise casually. So when he posted on X after watching a private screening of Salman Khan's upcoming war drama **Maatrubhumi**, calling it a "must-watch film," the industry took notice.

The film, formerly titled **Battle of Galwan**, has had one of the most turbulent journeys of any major Bollywood production in recent years. And for NRIs following from abroad, the story behind the story is as compelling as anything on screen.

## From Galwan Valley to 'May War Rest in Peace'

The project started as a dramatisation of the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash — the deadliest border confrontation between India and China in decades, which left 20 Indian soldiers dead in hand-to-hand combat at 14,000 feet. Directed by Apoorva Lakhia and starring Salman Khan in a military avatar, it was one of the most anticipated patriotic films in years.

Then the Defence Ministry stepped in. The government asked the production team to move away from a strictly factual account, concerned about the diplomatic sensitivity of naming China directly in a commercial film. The result: nearly 40 percent of the film was reshot. A fictional backstory was added. A romantic arc was woven in. The title was changed to **Maatrubhumi** — Hindi for "Motherland" — with a tagline that reads "May War Rest in Peace."

The pivots didn't stop there. The originally planned April release was shelved. OTT rumours swirled. Reports surfaced that the Censor Board was still reviewing sensitive portions. Through it all, Salman Khan and the production team maintained that the film would be a theatrical release.

## What Ghai Saw

Ghai's endorsement, while brief, was specific. He praised the film's "emotional depth" and "patriotic storytelling," noting that it portrays "the warm story of Indo-China soldiers and their respective emotions for their nations and families." That last detail is significant. The film does not take a purely confrontational stance — it humanises soldiers on both sides, a creative choice that reportedly emerged from the Defence Ministry-mandated rewrites.

For a film that has been through so many changes, Ghai's response suggests the final product has found its centre. His endorsement carries weight not just because of his stature, but because he is one of the few Indian filmmakers who has consistently navigated the intersection of patriotism and commercial cinema without losing the audience's trust.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Galwan is not abstract history. When the clash happened in June 2020, it dominated WhatsApp groups, dinner conversations, and social media across the US, UK, Canada, and Australia. NRIs followed every update, mourned the soldiers, and debated the geopolitical implications. A film about Galwan — however fictionalised — speaks to a diaspora that carries both pride in India's military and anxiety about its borders.

The question is whether Maatrubhumi can deliver the emotional weight of that moment while navigating the government-mandated constraints. Ghai's review suggests it can. But the real test comes when audiences see it.

## What's Next

The film's release date remains unconfirmed, though reports point to a window later this summer. Salman Khan is also involved with the delayed Sikandar and the ambitious mega-franchise film *Tiger vs Pathaan*. But Maatrubhumi is different — it's a prestige project, a film about sacrifice and duty, and the actor's most serious role in years.

The cast includes Abhishek Bachchan in a military role and Tabu as an emotional anchor. The production scale is described as massive, with battlefield recreations and advanced VFX work.

For now, the film has one important thing going for it: Subhash Ghai thinks it works. In Bollywood, that still means something.

*Sources: The Indian Eye, Bollywood Hungama, SacNilk*
